title: The guns at Outpost Snipe
photoNote: A 6-pounder anti-tank gun in the Western Desert, 29 October 1942, two days after Snipe. Imperial War Museum E 18802, British official photograph, Crown copyright expired, public domain. Supplied by Brian 24 Oct 2026 from the Wikipedia article (800 px). Not the Snipe position itself.
body:
Nineteen small antitank guns, dug into a desert hollow in the dark. At dawn the enemy's tanks came at them, and they kept coming all day.

27 October 1942. Four days into the Second Battle of El Alamein, the 2nd Battalion of the Rifle Brigade and a battery of Royal Artillery gunners held a position codenamed Snipe. Their guns were six pounders. Through the day, German and Italian tanks attacked again and again.

Their commander, Lieutenant Colonel Victor Turner, found one gun down to an officer and a sergeant, and joined them as loader. Between them they knocked out five more tanks. A shell fragment hit Turner in the head. He would not let anyone treat it until the last tank had been driven off.

A month later, a committee walked the ground and counted between 52 and 57 enemy armored vehicles knocked out around Snipe. Turner received the Victoria Cross.

Eight days after Snipe, the British broke through at El Alamein, and Rommel's army began its long retreat.

Nineteen small antitank guns, dug into a desert hollow in the dark. At dawn the tanks came, and kept coming all day.

27 October 1942, El Alamein. The Rifle Brigade held a position called Snipe. Their commander, Lt. Col. Victor Turner, joined one gun as loader and kept loading with a head wound until the last tank was driven off.

A month later, a committee counted more than 50 enemy armored vehicles knocked out. Turner won the Victoria Cross.

alt: Archival 1942 photo of a British 6-pounder anti-tank gun in the desert sand, a crewman leaning on its shield and another standing behind. Text: 27 OCT 1942, El Alamein, Egypt. Nineteen guns held.

video.note: Desert Victory (1943), British Ministry of Information documentary with film shot by the Army Film and Photographic Unit; Crown copyright expired, public domain (PD-UKGov on Wikimedia Commons; 480p copy from Brian's Source Film folder). From the film's Kidney Ridge section, which its narrator introduces as 'the fourth day of the battle' (27 October). The film does not identify Snipe, so the caption says it shows the Alamein fighting. Wide combat camera shots only; the staged close ups are left out. Clip uses 35:15.85 to 35:19.55, 35:27.30 to 35:28.70, 35:28.75 to 35:31.35, 35:34.15 to 35:36.15, 35:39.45 to 35:41.50, and 35:46.25 to 35:50.10. Sound: the film's own soundtrack under these shots (gunfire, shell bursts and shell whistle; no narration or music, checked by speech recognition and spectrogram), cut with the picture and normalized to -16 LUFS.
